summary: Discovery call to qualify Ironwood's interest in Redwood Dedicated reserved capacity. Ironwood is evaluating dedicated GPUs for low-latency inference across financial workloads; main concerns are data isolation, predictable throughput for market hours, burst capacity, and security compliance. Redwood AE+SE covered architecture, autoscaling options, quantization/tradeoffs, and next steps to run benchmarks and share pricing and security docs.
transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2026-03-04
Start time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Michael Stone (Ironwood - Head of ML Ops), Sara Lin (Ironwood - VP Eng), Derek Patel (Ironwood - Infra)

Summary: Quick discovery to understand Ironwood's inference needs, capacity expectations for dedicated GPUs, isolation/ compliance requirements, and next steps for a pilot.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, I'll kick us off. Alex from Redwood, AE, with Priya our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Michael Stone: Good, thanks. Morning all.
[00:10] Sara Lin: Hi, morning. We're excited to talk through dedicated options  want to make sure we cover isolation and burst behavior.
[00:18] Alex Chen: Perfect. Quick agenda: hear about your current stack and pain, talk dedicated reserved capacity model, burst/autoscale, security and timeline, and then next steps.
[00:27] Priya Rao: Hi  I'll dive into technical tradeoffs when helpful; especially around latency vs cost, batching, and KV cache behavior.
[00:33] Michael Stone: Cool. Quick context: Ironwood runs a set of real-time risk and client-facing summarization features. We have a mixture of high QPS during market opens and much lower usage overnight. Right now models run on a mix of in-house GPU infra and cloud endpoints but we're seeing variability in latency and some noisy multitenant interference. So we're exploring reserved capacity  want isolation and predictable p99s.
[00:57] Derek Patel: Yeah, and from infra perspective we need control over network egress, SSO integration, and we have a hard requirement for SOC2 type controls and audit logs.
[01:08] Priya Rao: Makes sense. For Redwood Dedicated we offer reserved GPU pools that are single-tenant; you get predictable throughput and isolation; we can colocate in a VPC or on-prem variant depending on your needs.
[01:20] Sara Lin: How does burst work? Some days we need 3x baseline capacity for short windows. We don't want to pay full reserved cost for peak.
[01:29] Alex Chen: Good question. We support a base reserved pool sized for your sustained needs plus a burst option. Burst can be configured as two flavors: internal burst within the same tenant onto pre-provisioned standby capacity (discounted commit) or cloud burst to the hosted fleet which is metered. We can propose a hybrid  commit to baseline reserved and allow metered burst during peaks.
[01:50] Michael Stone: What's the expected cold-start time when bursting to hosted?
[01:54] Priya Rao: If we fall back to hosted we typically route to a verified variant of the same model; cold-start depends on model size  for a 30B model you'd see an additional 200-800ms depending on kernel warms and cache; if we use warm standby in Dedicated it's sub-100ms.
[02:10] Derek Patel: We need SLA guarantees around p99 during market hours. Can Redwood provide that on Dedicated?
[02:16] Alex Chen: Yes, Dedicated comes with SLA-backed targets. We define market-hours windows and commit to p99 latency targets in contract. For mission-critical workloads customers often combine Dedicated with warm standby nodes to meet tight SLOs.
[02:29] Sara Lin: On security: we need SSO, RBAC, KMS integration for keys, and audit logs streamed to our SIEM. Also data must never leave our VPC.
[02:39] Priya Rao: We support SAML SSO and RBAC out of the box, KMS integration for model keys and encryption, and audit logs can be exported. For the VPC requirement we have a Private deployment that keeps data in your network or a VPC peering option for Dedicated. We should schedule a security deep-dive to map controls.
[02:58] Michael Stone: Good. What about model versions and rollouts? We do A/B testing and need canary rollback.
[03:04] Priya Rao: Dedicated supports pinned model versions, canary rollouts, and automatic fallback policiesso you can route traffic between model variants and have automated rollback if latency or quality regressions are seen.
[03:16] Sara Lin: Cost: our finance team will push back on reserved capacity cost. We need a clear unit economics case versus hosted.
[03:23] Alex Chen: Totally  we typically present per-token and per-hour numbers vs hosted; with batching and prefix caching Dedicated often reduces unit cost for steady baselines, while burst handles spikes. We'll include a pricing scenario for your peak/off-peak patterns.
[03:36] Michael Stone: Could you give an example? Say baseline 8x A100-equivalent devices and spikes to 24 for an hour twice a day.
[03:45] Priya Rao: For that pattern we'd propose 8 reserved, with either warm standby or metered burst for the additional 16 during spikes. Warm standby is more costly than pure hosted burst, but gives much lower p99. We can model the costI'd need your token/QPS distributions to run an accurate calc.
[04:03] Derek Patel: We can share a week of telemetry. We'll anonymize workloads.
[04:08] Michael Stone: We'll do that.
[04:10] Alex Chen: Great. Can you describe the workloads  avg token length, realtime vs batch?
[04:15] Michael Stone: Mostly realtime summarization and reranking. Typical request 250-600 tokens, we do reranks with 610 candidates. Latency target is 200350ms p99 across market hours.
[04:28] Priya Rao: For p99 200350ms on those request sizes you probably need fairly aggressive quantization and batching disabled for tail latency sensitive routes. Also KV cache and prefix caching can help if you have repeated contexts. We'll capture those tradeoffs in the benchmark.
[04:45] Sara Lin: How invasive is the Private deployment? Would we have to change networking or app code?
[04:49] Priya Rao: Private VPC deployment usually needs peering and routing changes, and we install a control plane component that integrates with your KMS/SSO. App integration is minimal  same Redwood API surface. On-prem is heavier but still uses the same API.
[05:03] Michael Stone: For regulatory reasons we may need the on-prem option for some clients.
[05:07] Alex Chen: Ok noted. We'll include both options in the materials.
[05:11] Derek Patel: How do you handle model compilation and kernel selection? We're running a mix of Llama2-derived and some in-house tamed models.
[05:18] Priya Rao: The runtime compiles and selects kernels based on architecture and sequence length distributions. For custom models we run a model onboarding that profiles perf and suggests quantization/compilation flags. There can be minor tokenizer/compat issues but we handle most of it.
[05:32] Michael Stone: Do you support local model storage behind our KMS? We can't upload plain model weights to hosted services for certain clients.
[05:40] Priya Rao: With Private or Dedicated VPC we can have customer-controlled model storage with KMS-managed encryption; we can arrange a signed process for model transfer.
[05:48] Sara Lin: What does the pilot look like? We want to validate p99 and unit cost over a 2-3 week period.
[05:54] Alex Chen: Typical pilot: 24 reserved GPUs sized for a slice of your traffic, run with shadow traffic or a percentage sample, run benchmarks using your payloads, measure latency and cost, and iterate. For your case I'd propose a 3-week pilot covering morning market hours.
[06:10] Michael Stone: Sounds reasonable. Who from Redwood will run the benchmark?
[06:14] Priya Rao: Priya (me) will run the benchmarks with help from our infra ops. We'll need your sample payloads and an SLO doc.
[06:21] Michael Stone: We'll share sample telemetry by Friday.
[06:24] Derek Patel: On networking, can we restrict egress? We need to prevent any model or data egress to public internet except specific S3 endpoints.
[06:32] Priya Rao: Yes, we can restrict egress in VPC deployments and lock outbound to allowed endpoints; we'll capture that in the security doc and the upcoming deep dive.
[06:40] Alex Chen: Anything else on compliance?
[06:43] Michael Stone: We need SOC2 Type II posture, data residency in US-East for some clients, and audit logs retained for 12 months.
[06:52] Priya Rao: We can provide SOC2 docs, and audit log retention is configurable; for Dedicated we can set retention and export to your SIEM.
[06:59] Sara Lin: Great. Regarding rollout — after pilot what's a typical timeline to full production?
[07:05] Alex Chen: Usually pilot 24 weeks, then plan for capacity reservation and contractual terms which can be 26 weeks depending on procurement. Could be as fast as 6 weeks end-to-end for simple cases.
[07:16] Michael Stone: Procurement will want pricing scenarios.
[07:19] Alex Chen: We'll include multiple scenarios: baseline reserved only, reserved + warm standby, and reserved + hosted burst. We'll show estimated unit cost and p99 impact.
[07:29] Priya Rao: One more technical note  for tail latency we recommend optional kernel-level optimizations and sometimes model quantization to 8-bit; we can discuss quality tradeoffs in the benchmark.
[07:41] Michael Stone: We'll want to compare quality before/after quant.
[07:44] Sara Lin: Any blockers from Redwood side for the pilot?
[07:47] Alex Chen: Need the anonymized telemetry, sample payloads, and a list of people for the security deep-dive. We'll send an intake form.
[07:55] Michael Stone: We'll get that to you.
[08:00] Alex Chen: Cool. Any final questions?
[08:03] Derek Patel: One small question: for audit logs can we stream to Splunk?
[08:06] Priya Rao: Yes, Splunk and S3-compatible endpoints are supported.
[08:10] Michael Stone: Fantastic.
[08:13] Alex Chen: Ok recap: Alex will send pricing and capacity layout by Friday (2026-03-06), Priya will run a benchmark after we receive sample payloads, and we'll schedule a security deep-dive for week of 2026-03-09. Michael to share telemetry and SLOs by 2026-03-05.
[08:31] Sara Lin: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[08:34] Alex Chen: Thanks  we'll follow up with links to docs and the intake form.
[08:38] 
[48:00] Meeting end

Notes: Transcript has minor transcription artifacts; speaker timestamps approximate. References: will share pricing spreadsheet, security pack (SOC2, KMS integration), and benchmark template.
